issues.legal_issue: A will surrounded by suspicious circumstances is not proved unless the propounder satisfies the court that it was duly executed and removes the legitimate suspicions.
material_facts: A beneficiary propounded a will to defeat a claim to a share in the deceased testator’s estate.

The will, allegedly made years before the testator’s death, was not disclosed until after the estate claim was being litigated; the beneficiary said he had discovered it by chance but gave no details of that discovery.
The will favored the beneficiary and excluded the testator’s wife and several close relatives, including on the basis of alleged misconduct for which no evidence was led.
The attesting witnesses were strangers to the testator’s family, gave contradictory accounts of the execution, and could not adequately describe the circumstances surrounding it.
The persons named as executors were available but were not examined.
The beneficiary did not explain the suspicious circumstances, and the High Court accepted the will without addressing them or applying the governing burden of proof.
issues.conclusion: The beneficiary failed to prove the will as the testator’s last will and testament. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the trial court’s judgment granting the estate claim was restored.
issues.legal_principle: A will must be proved like any other document by evidence satisfying the prudent mind, without requiring mathematical certainty. Under section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must be attested; as stated in the judgment, section 63 of the Evidence Act requires at least one available and capable attesting witness to be called to prove execution. Because a will speaks from the testator’s death and the testator cannot testify about its execution, proof carries special solemnity. Where suspicious circumstances surround execution, the propounder’s initial burden is heavier and the propounder must remove all legitimate doubts with cogent and convincing evidence before the will can be accepted. These principles were drawn from and applied in R. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma & Others.

rule.if: will_propounded_in_estate_share_dispute and will_disclosed_only_after_testator_death_and_late_in_litigation and propounder_claimed_accidental_discovery_without_details and attesting_witnesses_were_strangers_and_gave_conflicting_accounts and available_named_executors_were_not_examined and will_favored_propounder_and_excluded_close_relatives and propounder_offered_no_explanation_for_suspicious_circumstances

predicates.will_propounded_in_estate_share_dispute: A person relied on a purported will to resist another person’s claim to a share in a deceased person’s estate.
predicates.will_disclosed_only_after_testator_death: The purported will was not disclosed until after the testator’s death and after litigation over the estate was underway.
predicates.propounder_claimed_accidental_discovery_: The person relying on the will said it was found by chance but gave no details explaining how it was found.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_were_strangers_and_g: The people who attested the purported will were strangers to the testator’s family and gave inconsistent accounts of its execution.
predicates.available_named_executors_were_not_exami: People named as executors in the purported will were available but were not called to give evidence.
predicates.will_favored_propounder_and_excluded_clo: The purported will substantially favored the person relying on it while excluding the testator’s wife and other close relatives.
predicates.propounder_offered_no_explanation_for_su: The person relying on the purported will gave no explanation for the circumstances that raised doubts about its execution.

issues.definition: When a will is relied on in an estate-share dispute and the stated circumstances raise doubts that the propounder does not explain, the propounder fails to prove the will.
